SLIDE 1: GlobalCommerce

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
Good morning. My name is Jawad Ahmad. Today I am presenting GlobalCommerce, my EduQual Level 6 project. The project connects marketplace records, warehouse inventory, international orders, shipment tracking, demand forecasting and operational monitoring. I will first explain the business problem, then the design, and finally demonstrate one international order. The current implementation is a locally deployed proof of concept. Payments, exchange rates, trade charges and sales histories use simulated data; I am not presenting it as a production trading service.

SHOW / DO:
Begin on the title slide. Introduce yourself, look at the panel, and explain the purpose before listing technologies.

IF ASKED:
What is the project in one sentence? A shared operating workspace that connects an international order with its stock, shipment, forecast and service-health information.

FORMAL ASSIGNED TITLE:
Design and Implementation of an Enterprise Cross-Border Digital Commerce Platform for Marketplace Management, Intelligent Inventory Optimization, AI-Assisted Demand Forecasting, International Order Processing, Logistics Visibility, and Executive Commerce Analytics

SLIDE 2: The business problem

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
Consider a customer placing an international order. The merchant needs to know whether stock is really available, what the total cost is, and where the shipment is. If these activities are disconnected, staff must reconcile the information manually. GlobalCommerce brings these records together. Its intended benefit is better coordination and more informed replenishment decisions. This is a design objective, not a measured claim that the prototype has already reduced costs or stockouts.

SHOW / DO:
Use a simple example: a UK customer buys two units from the warehouse with sufficient available stock.

IF ASKED:
How would you prove business value? Measure baseline and post-pilot stockouts, fulfilment time, forecast error and manual reconciliation effort.

SLIDE 3: What the prototype covers

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The prototype has four connected responsibilities. First, it stores marketplace records. Second, it processes inventory reservations and international orders, with a shipment event history. Third, it forecasts demand and proposes replenishment quantities. Fourth, it presents business and technical information. The demonstration uses three warehouse locations and five supported currencies. It does not connect to live payment, carrier or customs services. The source and documentation remain local at present; GitHub submission is a separate step that I will complete after review.

IF ASKED:
Why a prototype? It permits an end-to-end demonstration and architectural evaluation within the student hardware and time constraints.

SLIDE 4: System architecture

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The browser runs a React-based console. It sends authenticated requests to a FastAPI application. PostgreSQL stores the business records, while Redis supports rate limiting. Forecasting runs in the application process. Prometheus collects service metrics, and Grafana visualizes those measurements. Docker Compose runs the six services. The design is a modular monolith at the application layer, not a microservice per business feature. This keeps deployment manageable on a 16 GB laptop. A future version could move heavy forecasting jobs to a separate worker and scale the API independently.

SHOW / DO:
Trace browser to API to database. Then trace API metrics to Prometheus to Grafana. Explain Redis separately from the database.

IF ASKED:
Why PostgreSQL? Orders, stock, payments and shipment records have relationships, and order creation needs transactional consistency. Why not microservices now? They add distributed failure and deployment complexity.

SLIDE 5: Inventory you can explain

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
On-hand stock means the physical quantity recorded in the warehouse. Reserved stock is committed to orders but has not yet been deducted on delivery. Available stock equals on hand minus reserved. In the illustrative example, 120 minus 3 gives 117 units available. The application locks the selected stock row and reserves stock within the order transaction. This is intended to protect against competing orders, but true concurrency behavior must be tested on PostgreSQL. The executive inventory card currently needs a calculation correction; the inventory table is the appropriate demonstration source.

SHOW / DO:
Use the equation, then point to the Inventory table in the live demo. These large example numbers are illustrative, not a screenshot measurement.

IF ASKED:
Why not deduct on hand immediately? Separating reservation from physical stock helps distinguish promised units from completed fulfilment. Cancellation and return rules need further work.

SLIDE 6: One order, one workflow

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The API validates the request and checks the idempotency key. A repeated key can return the existing order instead of intentionally creating another one. The system selects a warehouse based on available quantity and locks the stock row. It reserves the required units, computes the simulated charges, and creates the order, simulated payment authorization and shipment records in a transaction. If an error occurs, the database transaction should roll back. The current strategy does not optimize distance or shipping cost. Concurrent duplicate requests and cross-user key reuse require stronger validation.

SHOW / DO:
Follow the numbered sequence. During the demo, record the order ID and show the corresponding inventory reservation.

IF ASKED:
What does idempotency mean? Retrying the same logical request should not produce a second business operation. Explain why a client retry can happen after a network timeout.

SLIDE 7: International order costing

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
International processing needs more than changing a currency symbol. This prototype stores an order currency and calculates goods, shipping, duty and tax. Its shipping rule is twelve dollars plus three point two dollars per kilogram. Duty is five percent of goods value; tax is eight percent of goods value plus duty. These are demonstration formulas, not real customs advice or country-specific tax rules. Payment authorization and capture are simulated. Production would require jurisdiction-specific rules, payment-provider integration, rounding policies and reliable exchange-rate history.

SHOW / DO:
Open a demo order and identify its currency and separate charge fields. Never call the mixed-currency dashboard total audited revenue.

IF ASKED:
Why retain currency per order? A numeric amount is ambiguous without currency, conversion basis and rounding rules.

text:
SLIDE 9: Demand forecasting

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The model uses 120 days of synthetic sales history for each product and warehouse. Features include one-day, seven-day and fourteen-day lags, a shifted seven-day rolling average, weekday and trend. A Random Forest is trained using the earlier eighty percent of observations and evaluated on the later twenty percent. MAE measures the average absolute error in units; RMSE penalizes large errors more strongly. Multi-day predictions are generated recursively. The current one-step holdout evaluation is not a full backtest of the recursive seven-day workflow. The results show prototype behavior on synthetic data, not proven real-world forecast accuracy.

SHOW / DO:
Trace the stages, then show the actual MAE and RMSE produced by a run. Do not invent a percentage accuracy.

IF ASKED:
Why Random Forest? It handles nonlinear tabular patterns and runs on CPU. It still needs comparison with simple seasonal-naive and moving-average baselines.

SLIDE 10: From forecast to stock

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The replenishment recommendation is the maximum of zero and forecast demand plus safety stock minus available stock. Suppose the seven-day demand prediction is sixty units, safety stock is fifteen, and available stock is fifty. The recommendation is twenty-five units. These numbers are illustrative. In the implementation, safety stock is derived from residual variation and the forecast horizon. This is a heuristic, not a calibrated service-level guarantee. The system proposes quantities; it does not place purchase orders. A formal approval workflow, supplier lead times, minimum order quantities and purchasing integration are future extensions.

SHOW / DO:
Explain each term before reading the result. During the demo, compare a forecast recommendation with the relevant warehouse balance.

IF ASKED:
Can the model be wrong? Yes. New promotions, changing demand and poor data can invalidate the pattern. A person should review recommendations; formal approval is not implemented.

SLIDE 13: Security and accountability

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The project includes token-based authentication and password hashing. Some operations use role checks, input validation and audit records, and Redis supports request rate limiting. Authentication answers who the user is; authorization decides what they may do. A user having a token is not enough for safe access to every merchant record. Tenant ownership enforcement is incomplete. Before production, the project needs consistent object-level authorization, secure secrets, HTTPS, restricted network exposure, backup recovery tests and a formal security review. These controls do not mean the prototype is certified to an international standard.

SHOW / DO:
Explain one protected endpoint and an audit record. Do not display passwords, bearer tokens or local secret values in slides or screen sharing.

IF ASKED:
What is your biggest security gap? Consistent tenant and object ownership enforcement, alongside replacing demonstration credentials and exposed development settings.

SLIDE 14: Evidence before confidence

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
There are four automated test functions in the current suite. They cover a normal order journey, a repeated order key, forecast output and basic security behavior. A passing happy-path test does not prove correctness under concurrency or failure. The test suite uses SQLite, so it does not validate PostgreSQL row-lock behavior. I would add tests for simultaneous stock reservations, invalid shipment transitions, repeated delivery, unauthorized object access and failures during transaction creation. Forecast evaluation needs rolling, multi-day backtesting against baselines. No production load benchmark or real-business impact result is claimed.

SHOW / DO:
Before the exam, rerun the suite and keep the dated result. This slide describes test scope, not a claim of a fresh passing run.

IF ASKED:
What evidence is missing? PostgreSQL concurrency tests, stronger negative tests, load measurements, real-data model evaluation and a full live-demo rehearsal.

SLIDE 16: From prototype to production

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
The prototype connects the main workflow, but several issues must be addressed before production. Second, the backend needs stronger tenant ownership and shipment transition rules, including duplicate-delivery protection. Third, forecasting needs real data and realistic multi-day evaluation. Finally, production needs live providers, asynchronous jobs, backups and load testing. These are prioritized engineering tasks, not features I am claiming are already finished.

SLIDE 18: Appendix: design questions

SAY — suggested wording; adapt honestly:
